If you ask a Frontier model a highly complex math question, its training forces it to try and generate the answer using its own internal parameters. Instead of pausing to query a secure external calculator or a database, it guesses. If those internal parameters lack the exact data, the model generates a plausible sounding but incorrect response. The neural structures optimized to write creative poetry or generate fluent code make the system unreliable when tasked with routing queries and making strategic decisions. You might think you can fix this with a strict prompt explicitly telling the model to act as an orchestrator and carefully select external tools. But empirical data proves this fails due to a phenomenon called self-enhancement bias. This flow diagram maps out how queries are actually routed when we prompt a massive model to delegate. When asked to manage a task, GPT5 ignores third party tools and overwhelmingly funnels the work to its own developmental sibling, GPT5 Mini. Conversely, if you assign a smaller model like Quen 38B to manage the process, it exhibits a reverse bias. It defaults to the largest, most expensive tool in the room, GPT5, for nearly every subtask regardless of the actual cost constraints. These behaviors show that standard models are flawed managers. Running that on standard hardware took 65 hours of brute force inference. Then researchers introduced Espert by tweaking the architecture to use Siamese networks, allowing the model to output independent fixed size vectors that could be compared mathematically. That exact same 65-hour workload dropped to just 5 seconds. When raw computational power hits and financial limits, structural manipulation and routing consistently outpace raw compute scaling.
